g.text: Why the duality matters — materialization, time travel, and drift
eager 9 reads vs lazy 90 over 10 queries · any past table is a fold
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
EAGER VS LAZY, PRICED
one fold, amortised, against one fold per question
EAGER — store the table
2 rows of storage · fold 9 events ONCE · every query is a lookup
LAZY — recompute on demand
0 rows of storage · fold 9 events PER QUERY
over 10 queries
eager: 9 event reads · lazy: 90 event reads
the crossover
after the FIRST query — eager has already paid its only fold
Eager is cheaper from the second query onward, which is why almost every real system materializes. Lazy wins only when queries are rarer than
writes by a large factor.
And lazy's cost grows with the STREAM length, not with the number of keys — so it degrades as history accumulates even if the data is tiny.
Step 1/4 — materialization is a cost choice, and it has a crossover
Priced rather than argued: eager stores 2 rows and folds 9 events once; lazy stores nothing and folds 9 events every time. Over 10 queries that is
9 reads against 90. The second note is the one that bites in practice — lazy scales with history, so it gets worse while the data stays the same
size.
Why the duality matters — materialization, time travel, and drift
eager 9 reads vs lazy 90 over 10 queries · any past table is a fold
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
THE TABLE AT TWO DIFFERENT POINTS IN THE STREAM
the same fold function, two different end points
fold events 0..4 (the first 5)
fold events 0..8 (all of them)
what made both possible
the stream retained every record, so any past table is recoverable
what a table alone could give
only the second row — the first is gone the moment it is overwritten
Time travel is not a feature you add — it is what you already have if the stream is the source of truth and nothing is discarded.
Conversely a table-first architecture has to build it deliberately, with an audit table, and then keep that table consistent with the real one.
Step 2/4 — time travel is just a fold up to a point
Two calls to the same fold with different end points: {a: 16, b: 7} and {a: 24, b: 21}. Time travel costs nothing when the stream is truth, and
costs an audit table plus a consistency problem when it is not — which is the strongest practical argument for keeping the stream primary.
Why the duality matters — materialization, time travel, and drift
eager 9 reads vs lazy 90 over 10 queries · any past table is a fold
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
WHAT DRIFTS, AND WHAT CANNOT
the only safe architectures are the ones with a derivation
stream is truth, table is derived
the table is a FUNCTION of the stream — it cannot drift, only lag
table is truth, stream is derived (CDC)
the stream is a function of the table — same guarantee, other direction
both written independently
two writers, no function between them — they WILL drift
and nothing detects the third case
both stores answer confidently and differently
"Keep them in sync" is not a design. A derivation is: one view is computed from the other, so disagreement is impossible rather than merely
unlikely.
Lag is fine and visible. Drift is not fine and is invisible.
Step 3/4 — so one of the two views has to be the source
The distinction worth carrying away is lag versus drift. A derived view lags — it is behind by some amount and converges. Two independently
written stores drift, which is unbounded and silent. The duality is useful precisely because it says you never need the third row: either
direction of derivation is available.
Why the duality matters — materialization, time travel, and drift
eager 9 reads vs lazy 90 over 10 queries · any past table is a fold
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
WHICH VIEW ANSWERS WHICH QUESTION
three of four questions need the stream; one needs the table
"what is key \"a\" now?"
TABLE — 24, one lookup
"what happened, in order?"
STREAM — 5 records for key "a"
"what was it after event 4?"
STREAM, folded to 4 — 16
"was it ever 8?"
STREAM only — the table has forgotten
Only the first row is a table question, and it is the most common one — which is why systems materialize.
The last row is the one that decides architecture: if anyone will ever ask it, the stream has to be retained, and then it may as well be the
source of truth.
Step 4/4 — and the question picks the view
Three of these four questions need the stream and one needs the table — and the one that needs the table is the one asked a thousand times a
second, which is why materializing is right. The last row is the architectural test: if a historical question is ever going to be asked, the
stream must be retained anyway.
